snippet.title: Can the Green Transition Work for Workers?
snippet.description:
Robert Pollin challenges the myth that climate action hurts working people—and explains why a just transition must be at the heart of a global Green New Deal.

Learn more about Building a Green Economy:
https://peri.umass.edu/research-areas/environmental-and-energy-economics/building-a-green-economy/

@UMass.Amherst economist & @PERIeconomics Co-Director Robert Pollin presents a compelling case for a global Green New Deal that fights climate change without sacrificing jobs. He explains why the shift to renewable energy is not just technologically possible, but economically beneficial—creating far more jobs than fossil fuels. But without strong labor protections and guaranteed wages, pensions, and reemployment for fossil fuel workers, the transition risks political backlash. Drawing from work in West Virginia and beyond, Pollin outlines the real costs, benefits, and global financing strategies needed to meet the 2050 net-zero target—while ensuring no community is left behind.

snippet.title: Can Universities Survive Politics?
snippet.description:
"If you can survive Mao Zedong, you can survive anything. These universities will be around a long, long time."

Harvard professor and historian William C. Kirby explores the role of universities in a democratic society—and what happens when that role is threatened. Kirby draws on his sweeping global perspective to examine the political pressures facing universities today. From 19th-century Berlin to Cold War America to modern China, Professor Kirby reveals how higher education has both shaped and been shaped by state power—and why the independence of universities has never been more vital.

As new laws, culture wars, and geopolitical tensions close in on campuses around the world, Kirby warns that academic freedom is not guaranteed. It is something we must defend—again and again.

This interview draws on the themes of his acclaimed book, "Empire of Ideas: Creating the Modern University from Germany to America to China", which traces the rise of the research university and its future in a shifting global order.

Learn more and find the book at https://www.hbs.edu/faculty/Pages/profile.aspx?facId=409749

snippet.title: What Stories Can Teach Us About Aging
snippet.description:
We need a new approach to research—one rooted in trust, lived experience, and the stories data often overlooks.

Ruth Finkelstein, Executive Director of the Brookdale Center for Healthy Aging at Hunter College, challenges how we understand aging, health disparities, and inequality. She argues that traditional data leaves out crucial questions—like how families support each other, how people navigate life after incarceration, and what lived experiences actually shape aging outcomes. Drawing from her work with older adults and formerly incarcerated people, Finkelstein advocates for research that begins with listening, values qualitative insight, and is grounded in trust. Her work reveals how structural gaps in income, healthcare, and housing—not just age—define the realities of aging in America.

Learn more about her work at https://hunter.cuny.edu/people/ruth-k-finkelstein/

Early last week with the second signing of the Treaty of Versailles, the world uhh “presumably” put an end to the conflict in Iran.
This memorandum of understanding included a fourteen point checklist of conditions (with none of them being particularly favourable to average Americans) BUT the one that stood out the most was an allocation for at LEAST three hundred billion dollars to be paid by the US and its regional partners for the reconstruction of Iran. 
Now assuming that our unnamed “regional partners” can’t be convinced to pay for our mistakes, this would work out to almost $2,000 for every current American taxpayer, which has a lot of people raising a lot of very valid questions, chief amongst which is… 
Where could all of this money possibly be going? 
For context, the Marshall Plan, that rebuilt the entirety of Western Europe after the second world war, cost America around… $150 billion dollars when adjusted for inflation. 
Back then that was enough money to restore the economies of 16 countries after 6 years of the most devastating war in human history… today we are supposedly going to be putting up twice that that amont… to a single country… after less than 6 months… of what was “technically” never a war to begin with. 
Additionally, unlike the Marshall Plan, Iran is unlikely to become an ally, raising other questions about the less savory operations that this money might end up financing… 
It sounds bad… but to be fair the big flashy headlines have (either maliciously or incompetently) misguided most people on where this money is coming from, and where it is actually going… 
If you take the time to do this… and understand the actual mechanics of this plan… it actually… just ends up making the whole thing look even dumber than it already sounds...

snippet.description:
What does economic inequality look like when we account for gender identity, sexual orientation, and lived experience? Economist Lee Badgett shares decades of research into the economic lives of LGBTQ people—and what most data still gets wrong.
